Learned group matches

When you name a group, Eddy remembers what that kind looks like — its shape, texture and colour — and pre-names matching groups on later trays. Moving an organism out of a named group teaches it the opposite: that look doesn't belong to that kind. Everything learned stays in this browser.

Reference library: 30 taxa built in — blue-winged olive, flathead and spiny crawler mayflies; common and spring stoneflies; net-spinning, case-building and free-living caddisflies; midge, black fly, crane fly, mosquito, phantom midge and horse fly; water penny; riffle, predaceous diving, whirligig and crawling water beetles; hellgrammite; alderfly; dragonfly and damselfly nymphs; water boatman; giant water bug; crayfish; scud; aquatic worm; leech and freshwater snail. A group that closely matches a reference specimen arrives pre-named, marked “Reference match”. What you teach Eddy yourself always overrides the reference library, and forgetting below clears only what you taught — the built-in library stays. Eight entries (common stonefly, hellgrammite, flathead mayfly, black fly, net-spinning caddisfly, crane fly, damselfly, phantom midge) were reinforced in Oct 2026 with 19 specimens measured on real compartment-tray photos — the kind with one taxon per cell.

Separation self-check: Eddy also keeps labelled specimens from mixed-taxa photos — crayfish sharing a tray with a mayfly, a caddisfly beside a water boatman. The check replays Eddy's own grouping on them, one photo at a time; two different kinds landing in one group, or a specimen pre-named as the wrong kind, gets flagged.

Everything runs on this device — photos are never uploaded, and the sheet is written only to the file you link or download.

Eddy is a stonefly nymph from the Quittapahilla who got tired of watching students count his friends by hand at midnight, so he learned to do it himself. He now lives in your tray and counts everyone who passes through — no one gets missed on his watch.

How the counter works

Each spot is judged against the light around it, so a shadow across one corner neither merges nor erases organisms; touching bodies are split by shape, and a seamless pile is estimated from its bulk — but only when the blob's shape really says “several bodies”: a big single animal like a stonefly has one solid core however large it is, and is never estimated into pieces. Checking the dots is you verifying the count, which is what makes it trustworthy.

Groups & tally

every group is a tally row

One list, one tally: each group below is a row of the datasheet — its count is already in the row, so naming the group right there is tallying it. Nothing to reconcile afterwards. Pick a common name and the family, feeding group and tolerance fill in from the reference table (built on your 2025 datasheet — your sheet's values win). Not sure what something is? Identify with key or Identify with AI on the row fills it in. Add a row by hand only for a kind the photo didn't group.

Auto-group identical organisms

Eddy groups organisms by how they look — body shape (compact, round, sprawly), texture (smooth or segmented), and colour — with size counting for little, so a young one stays with its own kind instead of splitting off. It also remembers the groups you name: name a group once and look-alikes on the next tray arrive pre-matched. Anything that differs stays in its own group. Each group lands below as its own tally row, count included.

Count a photo first — grouping needs at least two dots.

K

Identify with the key

Built from the keys you sent. The HCTF Education Freshwater Macroinvertebrate Identification Key (photo key) and Key to Macroinvertebrate Life in the River (UW–Extension / Wisconsin DNR, developed at Riveredge Nature Center) ask the same questions in the same order — shells, legs, tails, wing cases — so they are merged here into one tap-through key covering 45 organisms. The Stroud booklet branches differently — it starts from the legs (10 or more, exactly 6, or none) — so it keeps its own tap-through below, covering 25 kinds down to order. Switch between them with the buttons; answer what you see on the specimen in front of you, and there is a Back button at every step.

One honest note on using these as a “data set”: the keys are a great rule set — the expert questions and the traits that separate one kind from another — and that is exactly what this view uses them for. They are not image training data for the recognizer in the Train view: each key shows one studio photo or drawing per kind (the Stroud booklet is all line drawings), and a model needs hundreds of real tray photos per kind. So the keys identify with you today, while your labeled crops in Train are still what will teach the model.

Pollution tolerance comes from the river key's colour dots: Sensitive Somewhat tolerant Not sensitive / tolerant — sensitive kinds are the ones whose presence signals clean water.

Looking up: just browsing — or tap “Identify with key” on any tally row and the answer fills that row in.

Water quality indices

Computed from each sample's tally — taxa richness, EPT richness (mayfly + stonefly + caddisfly taxa), the share of individuals that are EPT, and the Hilsenhoff Biotic Index on the 0–10 tolerance scale (lower is cleaner). Finished samples get a one-click printable lab report.

R

Train the recognizer

Automatic ID is learned from labeled examples — and you're already making them. Every time you name a group on the Workbench and finish the sample, Eddy saves a small photo crop of each organism in that group, tagged with the name you gave it. That's exactly the training data a recognition model needs, collected as a by-product of normal lab work.

The goal is about 200 crops per common name — enough for a first model. Once a few taxa hit that mark, download the set and it can be fine-tuned into a recognizer (a pretrained image model retrained on your crops, e.g. on a free Colab GPU) that suggests a name for each new group before you confirm it. Until then, Eddy is honest: it groups near-identical organisms, but you do the identifying.

About the big booklet you sent — Stroud Water Research Center's Identification Guide to Freshwater Macroinvertebrates: it can't add crops here, because every picture in it is a line drawing, and a photo recognizer can only learn from real photos — a sketch of a mayfly doesn't teach it what a mayfly looks like on your tray. What the booklet does have is a proper dichotomous key, so that is built into the ID Key view as its own tap-through key instead. Your tray crops below remain the training set.

What counts — and tips

What counts — Virginia Save Our Streams protocol

From the one-page VA SOS guide you sent. The counter dots everything dark on the tray — use this list when you check the dots: anything under “Don't include” gets its dot removed on the Workbench and no tally row.

Include in the count

  • Living aquatic benthic macroinvertebrates — the standard count.
  • Dead ones too, if they're mostly intact and still identifiable.
  • Anything that doesn't fit a category on the VA SOS datasheet: identify it if you can, tally it under “other benthic macroinvertebrates,” note the ID in the sample comments (the Notes field on the Workbench), and include it in the total count. Unsure of an ID? VA SOS suggests reaching out to the VA SOS Coordinator for help.

Don't include

  • Headless organisms and exoskeletons (shed skins).
  • Surface breathers — water striders, whirligig beetles, water boatmen, and predaceous diving beetles.
  • Terrestrial bugs that fell in.
  • Salamanders, fish, or other vertebrates.
  • Adults and pupae.
  • Empty caddisfly cases and empty shells.

Tips for a count you can trust

  • Light tray, even light. A white or pale tray under flat overhead light counts best. Shadows and hands in frame get dotted as organisms.
  • Spread them out. The gridded subsampling tray you're already using is ideal. A tight pile fuses into one blob — the counter estimates its head count from the pile's size, but spreading the pile out before the photo still counts better than any estimate.
  • Fill the frame with the tray. Tiny organisms in a wide shot get missed. Get close enough that the tray edges are near the photo edges.
  • Always verify the dots. The check strip turns green when your tally matches the dots. If they disagree, one of them is wrong — find it before you finish the sample.
  • Groups are near-identical matches, not IDs. Eddy groups strictly by size, shape, and tone in the photo — an organism joins a group only if it closely matches every member already in it, so different kinds stay apart. Each group is a tally row in the Groups & tally panel and shows close-up photos cropped from the tray: compare them with the key, and hover a group row to light up its dots and eyeball them. If a group still mixes kinds, open Adjust members on the row: select the odd organisms and split them into their own group, or move them into the group they belong to; dots that aren't in any group can be added from the same panel. Juveniles of one kind can also split across two groups — just give both the same name and they'll add up in the sheet.
  • Name groups carefully — you're teaching. Every named group becomes training data for the future recognizer (Train view). A group you mislabel teaches the model the wrong thing, so if a group mixes two kinds, split the odd ones out with Adjust members instead of naming the group after just one.
  • Stuck on an ID? Use the ID Key. It follows your keys exactly — shell or no shell, how many legs, how many tails, hard or leathery wing cases; the Stroud booklet key starts from the legs instead. If the key lands somewhere that doesn't match what you see, go Back one step: the trait you misread is almost always tails or wing cases.
  • No photo? You can still tally. Skip the tray photo and count by eye in the Groups & tally panel — the Excel download works the same.

Eddy — the macroinvertebrate counter. Counting and tallying happen entirely on this device; with a linked file the sheet updates itself in place, otherwise the only file that leaves is the Excel sheet you download.
